items.prompt: What is the correct order, and why?
options: Fetch → cache → hash, because caching first saves bandwidth
Parse → hash → cache, because parsed text is what claims quote
Fetch → hash → cache: hash BEFORE parsing so parser refactors never invalidate seen.json or old span anchors; cache AFTER hashing so files are content-addressed
Hash → fetch → parse, because hashes are inputs
items.explanation: Each step buys a specific property: the hash of canonical bytes survives parser changes; the content-addressed cache dedupes by construction. (obj-12-a)

items.prompt: Hashing AFTER parsing instead of before invites:
options: Nothing — parsed bytes are canonical bytes
Every later parser tweak silently invalidates seen.json (spurious re-notices) and breaks old anchors
items.explanation: Parse-then-hash couples your change-detection to your parser implementation — a refactor becomes a flood of false notices. (obj-12-a)

items.prompt: A receipt's claim cites a quote with span [412–481] in snapshot n8n-releases-5c9a4b7e.md. Months later a dispute arises. What makes this checkable NOW?
options: The content-addressed snapshot file (findable by hash) and the byte range: open, seek, compare — the anchor makes 'the source said this' falsifiable rather than a recollection
The judge's score is stored too
The snapshot is still hot in the actor's cache
items.explanation: Anchoring is the difference between citation and vibes: hash + span + preserved file = a dispute you can win months later. (obj-12-b)

items.prompt: On every receipt write, the system asserts span ⊆ snapshot. Why?
options: An anchor pointing outside its snapshot is a contract violation — it would break the very checkability the anchor exists to provide; it fails the build, not the receipt
items.explanation: The integrity of anchors is regression-tested like arithmetic: a broken anchor is a bug, not a shape we allow. (obj-12-b)
